transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Most nights after my wife goes to bed, I end up in the kitchen eating way more than a normal meal. Like fried chicken, mac and cheese, sweet potatoes, rolls—whatever leftovers are around. I’ll keep going until a whole tray is gone, or half the fridge is empty.
When you're eating during these nighttime episodes, are you fully awake and aware of what you're doing, or do you feel like you're not quite awake and later have trouble remembering it clearly?
I'm not really sure what you mean. I know I'm up in the kitchen eating, but I haven't paid much attention to how awake I feel.
The next morning, do you clearly remember what and how much you ate during the night, or do you sometimes have little or no memory of it until someone tells you or you see the evidence?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really thought about whether I remember all of it the next day.
When these episodes happen, do you remember consciously waking up and deciding to go to the kitchen, or do you just suddenly find yourself already there eating without recalling how you got there?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed whether I consciously decide to get up or not—I just know I end up in the kitchen eating.

Has your wife ever tried talking to you or interacting with you during one of these nighttime eating episodes? If so, do you respond normally as if fully awake, or do you seem confused, unresponsive, or 'out of it'?
I’m not sure. We haven’t really talked about whether she’s tried to interact with me while it’s happening.
During these episodes, are you able to do things like turn on the kitchen light, use plates and utensils, and avoid bumping into things just as you would if you were fully awake during the day?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid attention to whether I’m doing those things normally or not when it happens.
Before these eating episodes happen, do you actually fall asleep first and then wake up to eat, or do you often still be awake and simply haven't fallen asleep yet when you go to the kitchen?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really tracked whether I’ve fallen asleep first or if I’m still awake when I end up going to the kitchen.
Before you head to the kitchen, do you notice a conscious urge or craving for food, as if you're hungry and choose to get up and eat?
A lot of the time, no, I’m not really hungry. I might’ve eaten dinner with my wife already, and then later I still end up in the kitchen picking at leftovers until it turns into another whole meal.
How do you feel emotionally about these nighttime eating episodes afterward—do you feel upset, guilty, or embarrassed about them?
Yeah. Afterwards I feel sick with myself. People see me as organized and strong, and then I’m sitting there feeling ashamed and guilty, just disgusted that I let it happen again.
Have you ever woken up and found dishes, wrappers, or food out in the kitchen that you have no memory of preparing or eating at all?
I don’t know. I haven’t noticed anything like that, but I also haven’t really checked for it.
Do these eating episodes typically happen in the evening before you've even tried to go to sleep, or do they happen after you've already gone to bed and been asleep for a while?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really paid close attention to whether it’s before I try to sleep or after I’ve been asleep.
How is your appetite in the morning—do you usually feel hungry for breakfast, or do you tend to skip it or eat very little?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid much attention to whether I’m hungry in the mornings or how much I eat for breakfast.
Would you say that the food you eat during these nighttime episodes makes up a large part of your total food intake for the day, more than what you eat during breakfast, lunch, and dinner combined?

Yeah, I think it probably is. Most nights after my wife goes to bed, I’ll eat way more than a normal meal—fried chicken, mac and cheese, sweet potatoes, rolls, whatever leftovers are there. Sometimes I’ll go through a whole tray or half the fridge.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes recurrent episodes of consuming excessive food after his wife goes to bed, during which he is aware of being awake and in the kitchen (not confused, amnestic, or unresponsive, distinguishing this from a sleep-related eating disorder/parasomnia). The nocturnal intake constitutes a disproportionately large share of his daily caloric consumption, occurs without preceding physiological hunger, and is followed by significant guilt, shame, and self-disgust. These features are consistent with Night Eating Syndrome, classified under 'Other specified feeding or eating disorders' (F50.8), rather than a parasomnia (which requires impaired consciousness/amnesia) or an unspecified eating disorder.
